title: Limits for a Text Message API
prompt: A company sells an API that sends text messages for its business customers, such as login codes and delivery alerts. Each message costs money, and the phone carrier blocks the whole account for an hour if it receives too many. Design the rate limiting, using the full routine.
facts: About 5,000 business customers; each may send up to 10 messages per second, with bursts of up to 50 after a quiet time
The carrier accepts at most 2,000 messages in any one-second span, by its own clock, for the whole company; above that, it blocks the company's account for an hour
At peak, customers together try to send about 3,000 messages per second; reading a message's delivery status is a separate call, about 5,000 per second at peak
15 API servers behind a load balancer; a customer's requests may all arrive on one server. Accepted messages go on a queue; sending workers take them from the queue and send them to the carrier
Supplied: a dispatch pacer in front of the carrier sends at most a set number of messages in each 10 ms slice, counting retries, and needs no shared store

Measured: a shared in-memory store answers a small script within 1 ms, runs about 100,000 scripts per second, and acknowledges only after its replica has the change; if its main copy fails, the replica takes over within 2 seconds. An API server builds any response, including a 429, within 10 ms

Requirement: the carrier never receives more than 2,000 messages in any one-second span; each customer stays within 10 per second with bursts of 50, at all times, outages included; an accepted message reaches the carrier within 10 seconds; a refused send gets 429 with Retry-After within 100 ms
Requirement: status reads keep working during a store outage; new sends may be refused during a store outage, but the carrier and customer limits must still hold
scope: Rate limiting for sending messages and reading their status
Billing and the message content are out of scope

requirements: States the carrier's 2,000 in any one-second span and its one-hour block, the per-customer limit at all times, delivery within 10 seconds, 429 with Retry-After within 100 ms, and different behaviour for sends and status reads during a store outage
estimation: Store load: about 3,000 send checks per second, far under 100,000; status reads need no shared check

Carrier: pacing at 19 messages per 10 ms gives at most 101 slices × 19 = 1,919 in any one-second span, under 2,000; so at most about 1,900 sends per second can be accepted, and about 1,100 of the 3,000 per second at peak must be refused
Refusal time: a 20 ms store timeout plus 10 ms to build the response is 30 ms, within 100 ms
design: API (send returns accepted or 429 with Retry-After; status read), data model (a token bucket per customer and an admission limit for the carrier), a high-level design with a shared store, a queue and a paced dispatcher, and a deep dive on atomic counting, global versus per-node limits, enforcing the carrier limit where messages are sent, and the failure mode for each kind of call
data: Customer buckets updated by one atomic script in the store, so two servers cannot both pass a customer's limit; the carrier limit enforced at dispatch by pacing, counting retries, and admission kept at or below the paced rate so the queue stays short
Per-node or global admission, a store timeout, and fail-closed for new sends with no limiter on status reads, each with the reason
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions and a trade-off, such as: failing closed for new sends refuses customers during a store outage but keeps both limits; per-node admission shares avoid one store key but waste capacity when traffic is uneven; already accepted messages keep flowing through the pacer; a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, global admission. Requirements: the carrier never receives more than 2,000 in any one-second span; 10 per second with bursts of 50 per customer at all times; accepted messages reach the carrier within 10 seconds; 429 with Retry-After within 100 ms; status reads always available. Estimates: about 3,000 send attempts per second at peak; pacing at 19 per 10 ms allows at most 1,919 in any one-second span, so admission is capped at 1,900 per second and about 1,100 per second are refused; about 3,000 store scripts per second, far under 100,000. API: POST /messages → 202, or 429 with Retry-After; GET /messages/{id}. Data: in the store, a token bucket per customer (room for 50, 10 per second) and an admission counter per calendar second (at most 1,900), expiring after a few seconds. High-level: load balancer → API servers → store with replica; accepted messages → queue → sending workers → pacer → carrier. Deep dive: one atomic script takes a customer token and an admission slot together or neither, so two servers cannot pass either limit, and a customer on one server still gets its full 10 per second. The carrier limit is enforced where messages leave: the pacer sends at most 19 per 10 ms slice, retries included, so any one-second span holds at most 1,919. Because admission never exceeds 1,900 per second, the queue drains as fast as it fills and a message waits about a second, within 10. Failures: a store call that has not answered in 20 ms counts as unreachable; new sends then fail closed with 429 and Retry-After: 5 within 30 ms, so neither limit can be passed; accepted messages keep flowing through the pacer; status reads use no limiter. If the main copy fails, the replica, which has every acknowledged change, takes over within 2 seconds. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: new sends are refused during a store outage.

Design B, per-node admission. Requirements and estimates as in Design A: 2,000 in any one-second span, 10 per second with bursts of 50 per customer, delivery within 10 seconds, about 3,000 attempts per second at peak, pacing at 19 per 10 ms. API: the same calls. Data: customer token buckets in the shared store; each API server keeps its own admission limit of 126 per calendar second, 15 × 126 = 1,890 in total. High-level: the same queue, workers and pacer. Deep dive: customer limits use one atomic script in the store; the carrier side needs no shared count: per-server admission keeps the total at or below 1,890 per second, so the queue stays short, and the pacer at 19 per 10 ms guarantees at most 1,919 in any one-second span at the carrier, retries included. Failures: a 20 ms store timeout; new sends then fail closed with 429 and Retry-After: 5 within 30 ms, because local customer buckets could hand out allowance already spent in the store; accepted messages keep flowing; status reads are unaffected. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: when traffic is uneven across servers, some servers refuse while others have room, so fewer than 1,890 per second may be accepted even when there is demand.

assumptions: The pacer is the only path to the carrier
reference.design:
Requirements: the carrier never receives more than 2,000 messages in any one-second span; 10 per second with bursts of 50 per customer, at all times; accepted messages reach the carrier within 10 seconds; 429 with Retry-After within 100 ms; status reads always available; new sends may be refused during a store outage, but both limits must hold.
Estimates: about 3,000 send attempts per second at peak. Pacing at 19 per 10 ms gives at most 101 × 19 = 1,919 in any one-second span, so admission is capped at 1,900 per second and about 1,100 are refused. About 3,000 store scripts per second, far under 100,000; a few hundred KB.
API: POST /messages → 202 or 429 with Retry-After; GET /messages/{id}. Data: in the shared store, a token bucket per customer (room for 50, 10 per second) and an admission counter per calendar second.
Design and deep dive: one atomic script takes a customer token and an admission slot together or neither, so no two servers can pass either limit, and a customer whose requests all reach one server still gets its full limit. Accepted messages go on a queue; the carrier limit is enforced where messages are sent, by the pacer, retries included, because limits checked only on arrival say nothing about when workers send. Admission at 1,900 per second keeps the queue short, so a message waits about a second.
Failures: a store call that has not answered within 20 ms counts as unreachable; new sends fail closed with 429 and Retry-After: 5, within 30 ms, because guessing could break the customer limit; the pacer keeps sending what was accepted; status reads use no limiter. The replica holds every acknowledged change and takes over within 2 seconds. Summary: each requirement is met.
alternatives: Per-node admission of 126 per second on each server with customer limits in the store and the same pacer: no shared admission key, but capacity is wasted when traffic is uneven
Rejected: failing open for sends when the store is down, because customer limits could be passed
Rejected: a carrier token bucket with room for 2,000 checked only on arrival, because a full bucket plus its refill, or workers sending a backlog at once, can put more than 2,000 in one second
Rejected: reading and then writing counts in two steps, because two servers could both take a customer's last token
